description: The image displays a set of three pie charts, labeled "easy," "medium," and "hard," with a central bottom label "CoT," representing problem distributions based on correctness under different difficulty settings. Each of the three charts is divided into four slices corresponding to categories defined in a shared legend positioned to the right of the charts. The categories and their associated colors are N+K+ (teal), N−K+ (yellow-tan), N−K− (light orange), and N+K− (dark orange). In the "easy" chart, the proportions are 45.9% for N−K+, 40.6% for N+K+, 10.1% for N−K−, and 3.3% for N+K−. The "medium" chart shows 44.6% for N+K+, 44.3% for N−K+, 7.2% for N−K−, and 3.9% for N+K−. The "hard" chart displays 36.8% for N−K−, 36.2% for N−K+, 20.1% for N+K+, and 7.0% for N+K−. All charts include exact percentage labels directly inside their respective slices, and none of the segments are visually emphasized through exploding, offsetting, or bolding. Across all three charts, the slices are arranged in a consistent clockwise order starting from the top right: teal, yellow-tan, light orange, and dark orange.
caption_used: Problem distribution based on correctness under the w/ knowledge and w/o knowledge settings using CoT. The results indicate that while easier problems are primarily hindered by a lack of knowledge (N−K+ at approximately 50%), medium problems show a consistent dominance of reasoning-based errors (N−K− at 15%). For hard problems, the primary bottleneck lies in the inability to integrate geometric reasoning, as evidenced by the sharp decline in N+K+ to below 10%.
